Many thanks

messages.body_plain:
Adrian

Good question, but easy to put your mind at rest.

In constructing a simulation, specification needs to be made of the detection function the animals actually obey and a model the analyst fits to the observed data.  The two functions you mention perform these two jobs.  This recognises the reality that the analyst will not necessarily fit the true detection model.  The `make.ddf.analyst.list` can include more than one model, recognising an analyst will fit multiple models to a data set.

Hope that is clear.

Hello,

I was wondering about the CV reported in the DSM ouput (in this case using the var.gam function).  I had seen that this was based on dividing the SE of the estimate by the estimate. I also had a question about getting stratum level estimates from a full density raster.  For instance, if I predict a DSM to an entire ranch but am curious about pasture level density estimates, and associated variability, what is the best way to go about attaining these estimates?  I had assumed the mean density value for all cells within a pasture would correspond to the density for that pasture, but I'm not sure if this is correct, and further don't think this same approach would work for CV.  I had also thought to use the full ranch to make the DSM and then just create a prediction grid clipped to the extent of each pasture, thereby attaining a density estimate and variability for each pasture individually.

Any guidance on these issues is much appreciated.

Thanks,

John

Definition of CV: standard deviation is an attribute of a population, standard error is an attribute of a parameter estimate.  We are dealing with the latter when performing abundance estimation.  You are correct that to express CV as a percentage, simply multiply by 100.

Regarding estimation in a sub-region via DSM.  Your second approach (prediction grid consisting of the region of interest) ought to produce both the point estimate as well as a measure of precision of that estimate should work.

If I am standing at a point, surveying for birds, and one of my target species is perched at the top of a very tall tree, which distance do I measure: the distance to the bird at the top of the tree, or the distance to the tree itself, at eye level? On one hand I'm envisioning distance sampling involving two dimensions (thus I would measure to the tree at eye level), but everything I'm reading in the texts specifies that I should record the observer-to-organism distance. Nick

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Basic question about measuring distances for distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Nick

Section 11.1 of Buckland et al. (2004) and Section 9.5 of Buckland et al. (2015) discuss distance sampling in three dimensions.  As you say, in general the approach is to project the location of the animal onto a two-dimensional plane and measure the radial distance (if point transect sampling) between observer and animal on that  plane.  This simplification is adequate if the vertical height of the animal is small relative to the radial distances measured.

The tricky part comes if the distribution of animals in the vertical dimension is not uniform.  We assume distribution of animals with respect to transects is uniform by having a relatively large number of transects randomly placed on the landscape.  It is not possible to "randomly" place transects in the vertical dimension, implying that incorporating the third dimension requires some knowledge or model of vertical distribution of animals.

Hence, as a best approximation, project the animal onto the x-y plane and record that radial distance.

messages.body_plain:
Shawn

Happy to hear Guillaume's analysis was of use to you.  He deserves all the credit.

I can point you to some literature on your first point, but not to your second point.  In 2006 Prof Buckland published a paper in The Auk on conventional analysis of point transect sampling.  As part of that paper, he conducted a simulation study investigating (among other things) the effect of overlap of points such that most birds were detected from >1 point.  A quote from the results:

"For population 2, there was severe overlap between plots, so that most birds in the study area were detected more than once. On average, there were 356 detections from a population of 225 birds, of which only 100 birds were within the central 1-km square that was surveyed. Nevertheless, there was almost no bias in estimated bird density: true density was one bird ha–1, and the mean of the 1,000 estimated densities
was 1.0056 ± 0.0026 birds ha–1 (mean ± SE). There was also only mild underestimation of the standard error: true standard error (estimated by
the standard deviation of the 1,000 population size estimates) was 0.0815, whereas the mean of the 1,000 analytic standard errors was 0.0750."

messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am working with data from mammal line transects for two regions, and I want to know what the difference in abundance between the two sites is for various different groups of species. I have divided my species into 8 functional groups, and, using 'Distance2', I have come up with detection function models for each of the functional groups. Not all functional groups fit the same detection function, since some have very relevant covariates and others don't (e.g. for some species group size is very important, but others are only seen alone so group size is irrelevant). However I expect detection functions to be the same for each site, only actual abundance to be different, so detection function models are across both sites without site as a covariate. I now want abundance estimates for each region but I am hitting a couple of problems:

1. Some of the sample sizes are small for an individual site (e.g. large primates were seen in big groups every day at one site, and only one was ever seen at the other site. This is of course very important information but not very good for an abundance estimate). If I use

>abundance_estimate(ds.model.sp1, ~Region.Label) # Region label = Site

will I get abundance estimates for each site without having to model each site and functional group separately?

2. I haven't been able to test the above because one of the sites has varying Areas since some of the transects were shorter than others. This seems to be throwing the function off. Should I manually divide group size by Area before setting out to resolve this? Or is there a clever way that Distance2 can deal with this?

Thanks in advance,
Kirstie

messages.subject: Conceptual issues - 3D sampling of mistletoes in forests
messages.subject_clean: Conceptual issues - 3D sampling of mistletoes in forests
messages.body_plain:
I want to use distance methods to sample mistletoes in forests in central Victoria, Australia. I have a number of conceptual questions - Rather than sampling a planar area, I'm actually sampling a 3 dimension space - how do i deal with mistletoes growing directly overhead?
If i project every mistletoe occurrence onto a horizontal plane for the purposes of calculating distance, then a mistletoe growing at 35 metres above my head has a distance of 0 metres, with an assumed detection rate of 100% , which is not practically achievable. If I use the actual distance, then I will need to use actual distance for every other mistletoe as well - my survey 'area' is then a volume, in the shape of a half cylinder, but truncated above at the limit of the canopy height.
This might also breach the random positioning of transect assumption - mistletoes are actually more likely to occur at the edge of the canopy than close to the ground, so every transect I do will be somewhat biased in terms of its positioning.

I imagine I'm not unique in this  - surveying for birds in forests, arboreal mammals, butterfies etc must have run into similar issues. Has anyone solved this issue?

gm

Hi Gregg, list,

To add to Eric's thoughts, doing it in 3D is much harder in practice - it's not a coincidence that people simplçy haven't really done it in practice. Therefore, I would possibly still project distances to the ground. Naturally, given that your object of interests might be 30 m up (and hence missedeven if on the line), you should consider a mark recapture distance sampling (MRDS) approach to estimate g0 (i.e. the probability of detection on the line).

You have the luxury of dealing with objects that move relatively slowly (MRDS methods are typically used with marine mammals, and these are quite faster than most immobile mistletoe ;) and therefore you could even completely change the game: still have a single observer protocol and set up independent trials to estimate g0. This is akin to say incorporating an independent estimate of g0 for burrowed desert tortoises, or some such. Feel free to contact me on the side if you think this is a potential way to go and you'd like to discuss it further.

T

Hi all,

I'm new to distance sampling and the Distance program. I have a few questions I would like some help with/correction if I have misunderstood some things.

I have used Distance to calculate density estimates for seven primate species. I did a separate analysis for each species. I have 5 study sites with different hunting pressure (one with high, two with intermediate, and two with low hunting pressure). The number of transects vary in each strata, so does the total survey effort per transect and total survey effort per strata. I have stratified by study site, so I have five strata, and a separate detection function for each strata. Except for one species at one study site were I only had three detections. For this one I used a global detection function to obtain density estimates at that study site, and used separate detection functions on the other study sites. Does this sound right?

When I chose size-bias regression method to estimate the cluster size, the majority of species in each strata got the warning "Size bias adjustment has increased expected cluster size". It does not seem to cause any problems for most of them as the adjustment is not that big, but for some species at some strata, the adjustment is unreasonably high. Is is reasonable to to choose size-bias regression for some strata and not for others (for the species were the size-bias adjustment caused a problem)?

I would like to compare the density estimates for each study site (per species) to see if there are any differences. I can see the trends from my estimates, but I want to test to see if there are any statistical significant difference. I have read that people with only two strata use the z-test, but do you have any suggestions for what I should do when I want to compare five? To compare those five, I'm assuming that I have to get the density estimates from each transect, but I do not have big enough sample size at each transect to fit a separate detection function, so these transect estimates will rely on the same detection function by strata.

Hope this is understandable.

Thanks,
Liss

Liss

You are asking advanced questions for a novice.

Your approach of using sites as strata producing unique detection functions for each stratum seems fine.  The species/site combination where you had only three detections is probably too small to say anything useful about density; you could use the global detection function there, but even then I would hope that the uncertainty in that estimate will be large (to reflect the paucity of data for that species and site).

Regarding your size-bias adjustment.  Step away from the computing issue for a moment and ask whether your estimate of group size is an accurate depiction of group size of your study species.  For some species, the average group size in a distance sampling survey is not an unbiased estimate of group size in the population because you tend to miss small groups at large distances.  Ask yourself whether this is the case for your species and study area; plot group size as a function of perpendicular distance; is there an absence of small groups at large distances?  If not, then you need not use the regression approach to adjust observed group size for size-bias.  I have no experience trying to estimate group size of primates in their native habitat, but biologists to do have that experience tell me it is quite difficult to determine the definition of "groups"; resulting perhaps both in inaccurate group size and inaccurate location of the group centre.  That may have something to do with your data suggesting an under- rather than over-estimate of average group size.  Consult the attached J. Primatology paper by Buckland et al. (2010) where they performed a simulation study showing that analysing primate data where each individual and their distance from the transect is recorded; consider that as an alternative analysis.

Finally for your contrasts between sites.  I don't pretend to know your research objective, but perhaps it is not difference between sites that is of interest (of course density is not exactly equivalent between any two sites), but you do mention hunting pressure.  Possibly you might with to perform contrasts between high:intermediate, high:low, intermediate:low pressure.  Then you could consider pooling your two intermediate sites (producing a single density estimate), likewise the two low sites (single estimate), then performing the three contrasts I mention in the previous sentence.  Possibly other readers of the list may have other suggestions for you here.

Thanks for the thorough testing Carolin.

There are some subtle issues associated with summarize_ds_models() because that function is usually used for the purpose of model selection.  To compare models (using AIC), the data used in the two models needs to be identical--otherwise the comparison is invalid.  When data are not binned, the data used for multiple models is identical, therefore the AIC comparison is legitimate.

However, when binning occurs, the summarize_ds_models() function should also test whether the data used in the models being compared is identical.  At the moment the function does not do that.  In the second example you provided, the function should prevent you from comparing models fitted to unbinned and binned data (the result is invalid).  The function should undertake that prevention in a nicer fashion than generating an error message.

To summarise, we should put a warning onto summarise_ds_models() that for the moment, it should only be used with models fitted to exact distance data.  In a future version, the function should be more clever and come up with a comparison that if binned data are used, ensuring the cut points are identical.  Likewise the function ought to check that the truncations distances for data in the models being considered is identical.  Those checks are not yet in place so the user needs to police themselves.

I'll raise an issue about this problem on our software development system.  Thanks for spotting this.

Caroline

Every analyst will want their own summaries of the analyses they have performed, so there is no generalised function beyond 'summarise_ds_models()' for that purpose.  Your "rbind()" effort is as good as any method for your purposes.

R is lovely for providing the tools to make functions out of repetitive calculations.  If you wish to have a summary of effective strip width, you could finish the function you began like this

ESW.calc <- function(my.ds.object) {
#  calculates effective strip width
#    given object created by function ds() of class "dsmodel"
#    Rexstad, 28Apr17
  if (class(my.ds.object) != "dsmodel") stop("Argument is not of class dsmodel")
  my.summary <- summary(my.ds.object)
  truncation <- my.ds.object$ddf$meta.data$width
  average.p <- my.summary$ds$average.p
  esw <- truncation * average.p
  return(esw)
}

If you want a vertical line placed at ESW on your detection function plot, try

plot(minke1)
ESW.for.hn <http://ESW.for.hn> <- ESW.calc(minke1)
abline(v=ESW.for.hn <http://ESW.for.hn>, lwd=2)
